articles.title: Philip Lustre seeks transfer of cyber libel case from Davao City
articles.summary: The camp of veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr., on Wednesday said they will ask that the cyber libel case against him be transferred from Davao City.

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 10:23pm
The camp of veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr., on Wednesday said they will ask that the cyber libel case against him be transferred from Davao City.

“For the court, we are in the course of filing the necessary pre-arraignment remedies including a motion for reinvestigation, motion to quash, and to of course transfer the venue because we do not feel safe in Davao City,” Lustre's lawyer Dino De Leon said in a press briefing.
He added that this is “considering the known proclivity of the Duterte family for violence.”
Police officers arrested Lustre in Quezon City on Saturday on the strength of a cyber libel arrest warrant issued by a court in Davao City.
De Leon later said that the complainant is lawyer Manases Carpio, the husband of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Lustre has been temporarily released after posting bail.
De Leon said he has also asked Davao City Prosecutor Jhopee Avanceña to confirm her ties to Honeylet Avanceña, the partner of former president Rodrigo Duterte.
National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag earlier said that Jhopee Avanceña and Honeylet Avanceña are cousins.

“Kami talaga ay nagugulat na pinirmahan niya ito kung related talaga siya kay Honeylet na kinakasama, longtime partner, in fact the de facto first lady nung mga panahon ni Rodrigo Duterte,” De Leon said.
(We are really surprised that he signed this, if he is indeed related to Honeylet, his live-in partner, longtime partner, and in fact, the de facto first lady during Rodrigo Duterte’s time.)
“We are asking for the record and, formally, we already wrote to the city prosecutor to confirm his relationship with Honeylet Avanceña,” he added.
He said they are also asking the prosecutor’s office for proof of service that subpoenas and summons were sent to Lustre.
De Leon said they are also asking the prosecutor’s office to show the efforts made to determine Lustre’s correct address.

Lustre’s camp previously said it was looking into what appeared to be a violation of his right to due process during the preliminary investigation, as he had neither been served nor received a subpoena or notice.

Prosecutor General Richard Fadullon also said that Lustre was denied due process because he was not given the opportunity to respond to the complaint before an arrest warrant was issued against him. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Is Iran headed to war or peace after Mecca alliance meeting?
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey have taken their latest peace push directly to Tehran. Officially, it was to avert a new military escalation, but their diplomatic outreach can also be seen as a…

image.caption: Senior officials from Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia all traveled to Tehran to meet President Masoud Pezeshkian and other Iranian leadersImage: Iranian Presidency/AFP

blocks.text: Amid rising fear that the US and Israel are preparing to launch new attacks on Iran after the US midterm electionon November 3, three major Middle Eastern powers delivered a coordinated diplomatic message directly to Tehran.

Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir, Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin all traveled to Iran to meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and senior officials in Tehran this Monday. The three envoys serve as representatives for the Mecca defense pact — a military alliance of Islamabad, Riyad and Ankara, which was officially set up this summer.
Saudi Arabia said ⁠the ⁠trip aims to open negotiating channels and "prevent the return of military escalation." Details on the agenda, however, remain scarce.
Iran conflict: Could a new phase of the war be imminent?

A senior Pakistani official cited by the Reuters news agency said the talks focused on building a regional non-aggression network, in addition to US-Iran talks, Houthi rebels' attacks on Saudi Arabia, the Strait of Hormuz and the US naval blockade.

Another official said Pakistan's Munir presented Iran with a solution to the conflict that would offer something both to Washington and Iran, with the three Mecca states and Qatar acting as mediators. The source told Reuters US President Donald Trump previously gave Munir the go-ahead to try diplomacy.
Tehran presents the meeting as a success
Iran hailed the "very positive atmosphere" during the Tehran talks, even though no breakthroughs were officially announced.
"Very good discussions took place between us," Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told state television. "I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region."
Rezaei argued that regional security should be built by countries in West Asia themselves and without outside intervention.

A day later, Rezaei reportedly met Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Iranian state media said Khamenei called for protecting Iran's interests and maintaining Tehran's conditions for ending both the war and the current state of "neither war nor peace."

Meanwhile, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian travelled to Moscow for the Gas Exporting Countries Forum, where he met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, with Pezeshkian and the emir also discussing the war and the Strait of Hormuz.
These and other diplomatic contacts were framed by Tehran as evidence that the US is unable to diplomatically isolate the Iranian regime.
Are Turkey and Pakistan closing ranks with Saudi Arabia?

The united front presented by the three nations in Tehran, however, can also be seen as a show of force for the new Mecca defense alliance. It comes as the Saudis grow increasingly wary of the attacks on Saudi infrastructure launched by the Iran-allied Houthi militants.
Egypt ready to back Saudi Arabia's war against Houthis

Under the terms of the Mecca agreement, an outside attack on one of the member states is to be regarded as an attack on all of them. The visit also came on the same day as Egypt's parliament agreeing to give military help to Ryad and take "all necessary measures" to help Saudi Arabia defend itself, in addition to the looming threat of the US and Israel.

"The presence of the three senior representatives at the same time sent the message that these countries are acting as a bloc," Babak Dorbeiki, a London-based political analyst and former official at Iran's Strategic Research Center, told DW.

Saudi Arabia has long been regarded as Iran's archrival in region. It has used its enormous wealth to counter Iran's influence, and now it can, at least in theory, also count on Pakistan's nuclear capability, and Turkey's conventional military strength.
At the same time, Dorbeiki argued that the Mecca pact is primarily designed for deterrence rather than offensive war. And defense pact does not mean its members want to fight Iran.
Dorbeiki believes the message from the bloc could therefore work in two directions: it can provide mediation, but continued escalation could also alter that position.
Ryad pushing for a 'diplomatic solution'

Saudi Arabia faces the most immediate dilemma. Further Houthi attacks damage its infrastructure and economy, but a wider war with Iran could threaten the investment and development projects at the heart of Riyadh's economic strategy.
"For Saudi Arabia, both the current situation and a war with Iran carry serious costs," Dorbeiki said. "Its preferred route is, therefore, a diplomatic solution."
What now for Saudi Arabia after Riyadh airport attack?

Moreover, Pakistan has spent months mediating between Washington and Tehran and has important relations with both. A direct conflict would also distract Islamabad from its long-standing security concerns involving India.

Turkey is a NATO member, but Dorbeiki says direct military support for Iran against the United States is highly improbable. The fact that Ankara sent intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin rather than its foreign or defense minister also suggests a cautious approach.
Iran pursues diplomacy while preparing for fighting
Ali Asghar Shafieian, media advisor for Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, also rejects the perspective that the Mecca pact representatives were trying to present Tehran with an ultimatum.
He told DW that the three countries may also have wanted to demonstrate their own growing coordination, while showing that Iran remains part of regional diplomacy.
"You cannot conclude from this meeting alone that it was an ultimatum before an attack," Shafieian said.
He also noted that Iran, just like the US and Israel, could prepare for the possibility of further conflict while maintaining negotiations.
Mediator or enforcer? Pakistan's role in the Middle East
"Just as they use the opportunity to strengthen their military and defensive capabilities, Iran does the same," he said.
Shafieian said an agreement remains possible if Iran's political standing and what Tehran describes as its national dignity are respected.
Diplomatic game continues
Analyst Dorbeiki argues that Iran is following a familiar strategy of extending negotiations while avoiding real-world commitments.
The Houthi rebels are central to Tehran's calculation.

Tehran has not publicly offered the kind of guarantees over Houthi attacks that Riyadh would want. Dorbeiki believes Iran could seek to trade influence over such the attacks for concessions such as an end to US military pressure and broader steps toward ending the war.
The only apparent outcome of the Tehran meeting is to keep talking. For Iran, that might be enough of a signal that it is still a diplomatic partner rather than an enemy.

articles.title: OBR slashes UK growth forecast for 2027 despite Healey’s budget measures
articles.summary: Outlook for living standards also downgraded as part of impact of Middle East conflict on economy

blocks.text: Britain’s economy has taken a multibillion-pound hit as the war in the Middle East drags down growth and triggers a fresh cost of living crisis, according to the government’s independent forecaster.

In a report as John Healey announced his first budget, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) issued a sharp downgrade for growth, living standards and the public finances despite the measures taken by the chancellor.

Although Healey sought to cushion the blow through “breathing space” policies to help households and businesses with soaring energy costs, the watchdog slashed its growth forecasts for 2027 and warned that inflation was poised to reach close to 4% as Britain’s early resilience to the war fizzles out.
While growth this year was upgraded from 1.1% to 1.2% after an unexpectedly resilient performance fuelled by AI investment, the watchdog slashed its estimate for next year from 1.6% to 1%.

Highlighting the damage from Donald Trump’s war in the Gulf, Healey said the exchequer was spending £14bn more on debt interest as the financial market fallout from the conflict pushes up borrowing costs for governments worldwide.

Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, the chancellor said he would allow a hit to his buffer against the government’s fiscal rules – while also announcing a temporary rise in tax on banks to fund his package of energy support.

He left £15bn of headroom against the main fiscal rule, which requires day-to-day spending to be matched by tax receipts in three years’ time – down from £23.6bn left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, in the spring.
As a consequence, the OBR said borrowing was poised to fall to about 2% of GDP in the medium term but at a slower near-term pace than previous plans.

As the energy price shock rippling out from the Middle East hits households and businesses, the OBR said consumers would face inflation of 3.5% this year, significantly higher than the 2% forecast in March.

Healey made helping families with the cost of living a core focus of his first budget, including £100 in blanket payments for 20 million households at a cost to the exchequer of £2.6bn and a plan to abolish standing charges on gas bills.

But despite their measures the OBR warned households would come under sustained pressure, with per person disposable incomes taking account of inflation expected to fall in the short-term, before rising modestly before the end of the current parliament.
Setting the stage for a tough election run-up for Labour, the watchdog said income levels would only be about 2% above pre-pandemic levels by the start of the 2030s.

Britain’s economy had shown more resilience than had been expected at the start of the Iran war, after recording the strongest rate of growth in the G7 in the first half of 2026. Official figures suggested a strong expansion in AI-related business activity as one factor behind the surprise rise.
after newsletter promotion

Healey sought to use his budget to harness the power of the technology to boost growth in future while also safeguarding the country against the risk of cyber-attacks amid the accelerating global AI race.

Although saying he would never be complacent, Healey said there were “signs of resilience” in the economy as he highlighted that the Bank of England and International Monetary Fund had issued upgraded growth upgrades for the UK within recent months.
“There are real challenges ahead but Britain has beaten the forecasts this year, and with the action I am taking today I believe Britain can beat the forecasts again,” he said.

However, the economy is coming under mounting pressure from the energy price shock triggered by the war. Since the start of the US-Israeli led invasion of Iran at the end of February, which has throttled energy flows in the region, oil prices have risen from about $70 a barrel to more than $115, while gas prices have almost tripled.

With a tentative pause in the fighting while Donald Trump prepares for crunch midterm elections, the OBR said the outlook for the economy, households and the UK public finances remained highly uncertain.

Suggesting there were “significantly better or worse outcomes of broadly equal probability”, it said that if energy prices were to rise to a higher and more sustained peak, government borrowing could be £17bn above the central forecast next year. However, a lower energy price path could reduce borrowing by £12bn.

articles.title: Mans Carpio is 'aggrieved party' in cyber libel case vs. Philip Lustre, says spokesman
articles.summary: Atty. Manases Carpio is the aggrieved party in the case against veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr., the former"s spokesperson said on Tuesday.

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 10:18pm
Atty. Manases Carpio is the aggrieved party in the case against veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr., the former’s spokesperson said on Tuesday.
Lawyer Neil Abayo, a spokesman for the husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, refuted accusations that the libel case against Lustre was an act to silence the press.

“Kung hindi siya nag post ng malicious and baseless possible libelous statement, hindi mangyayari na makakasuhan ang isang individual,” Abayon said. (If he did not post the malicious and baseless possible libelous statement, an individual will not be faced with a case.)
“Atty. Mans is actually the aggrieved party here considering it is the respondent who committed the possible criminal act,” he added.
Abayon also refuted claims that the warrant was rushed and operated, saying that the complainant had nothing to do with the implementation of a warrant, as it depended on the police.
In a Facebook post on Sunday after he posted bail, Lustre said that warrant was deliberately served on a Saturday so he could stay in jail over the weekend since he could not post bail.

“If they will insinuate wrongdoing, they must show evidence to back up their allegations of bad faith or malice on the part of the law enforcement authorities. Otherwise, that will remain as baseless allegations and could taint the reputation of men in uniform who are simply doing their job,” Abayon said.
Carpio’s spokesperson also said that Lustre should address his admission that there were “backroom moves” when it came to the posting of his bail.
Last Sunday, Lustre announced that he had posted bail by using “backroom moves”.

Lustre’s arrest came only a day after Davao City lawmaker Paolo Duterte lodged libel complaints against GMA Network journalists and executives. The two incidents lead to media groups raising concerns over press freedom.

“It was definitely a special operation against me. The intention was to have me arrested on a Saturday and stay in jail on a weekend because I might not be able to post bail for my release. There was procedure flaw in the process. That was how deep the Davao Group do their thing,” Lustre said. —Jean Mangaluz/NB, GMA News

articles.title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr
articles.summary:
Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website

Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the…

blocks.text: Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.
Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.
According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups.

“Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.
Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.
Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions.

Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – follows the arrest of the entire six-person team at the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom.

blocks.caption: Lina Attalah holds a meeting in the Mada Masr office in 2015.  Photograph: Sabry Khaled/Sabry Khaled For The Guardian

blocks.text: The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing.

“This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.”

According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”.

Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict. Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”.

Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November.
Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen International issued a statement with several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves.

“Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.”

articles.title: Menindee Lakes water levels drop to lowest in five years as experts warn of mass fish deaths
articles.summary: NSW government imposes water restrictions after Menindee water volumes fall below 2021 levels
articles.byline: Lisa Cox Environment and climate correspondent

blocks.text: Water levels at Menindee Lakes in western New South Wales have fallen to their lowest point in five years, prompting the state government to impose upstream water use restrictions as experts warn of potential mass fish deaths over summer.
Combined storage at Menindee Lakes fell below 480 gigalitres earlier this month, the first time since 2021.
In the upper Menindee Lakes, water volumes have dropped below 250GL, a level that triggers temporary state water restrictions across parts of the northern Murray-Darling basin.
The restrictions limit access for some irrigators and are intended to preserve water for critical human needs and the environment.

It follows periods of low rainfall in the catchment throughout the past 12 months, with experts warning of a growing risk of summer fish kills unless flows down to Menindee Lakes via the Darling-Baaka River improve.
Menindee was the site of catastrophic fish kills in 2018, 2019 and 2023, which saw millions of dead fish wash up along stretches of the Darling-Baaka.

“Government officials are predicting with a level of certainty that unless there’s more water flowing into the Baaka-Darling River that there will be fish kills at Menindee this summer,” said Prof Jamie Pittock of the Australian National University and the Wentworth Group of Concerned Scientists.
“We need a major rainfall event to happen and for the state governments to prevent irrigators from pumping out the first flush of water.”
Graeme McCrabb, who was one of the first Menindee residents to raise the alarm about the 2018-19 disasters, said the combined Menindee Lakes had reached “drought reserve volumes”.
He said this effectively meant conservation of water “at all costs”. McCrabb said he was hopeful that recent rainfall in Queensland may result in some replenishment of the Menindee system.
“There are some small inflows coming across the Queensland border now which probably give us some hope for the summer. But we would need more on top of that,” he said.
“If we don’t get inflows, the risk [of fish kills] would be very high in January or February.”
He said a milder summer would also lower the risk.
after newsletter promotion
“I’m worried about fish kills to be honest,” McCrabb said.
“It’s a tough time or sad time when the water starts to get that real green algal look.”
Days after winning the 2023 state election, the premier, Chris Minns, and senior state ministers visited Menindee and committed to an investigation of the mass fish kills.

An expert panel was established under the northern basin connectivity program, which recommended limiting upstream overextraction during dry periods, to help maintain flows in tributaries into the Darling-Baaka River to Menindee Lakes. This was to try to reduce the risk of catastrophes such as fish kills and large-scale drying.
The panel delivered its final report two years ago but the state government is yet to implement it.
McCrabb said he was disappointed the government had not followed through on the recommendations of the connectivity panel.
“Since the fish kills, government agencies have made no policy changes to improve water quality outcomes,” he said.
Comment has been sought from the NSW water minister, Rose Jackson.

articles.title: An update on CBC’s plans to open new world bureaus
articles.summary: New bureaus in China, Mexico and Berlin will soon add to CBC News's efforts to deliver international reporting by Canadians, for Canadians.

image.caption: CBC war correspondent Matthew Halton prepares to broadcast in Sicily, Italy, on Aug. 20 1943. CBC had launched its own news division just two years earlier, ending its reliance on dispatches by The Canadian Press. (CBC)

blocks.text: Editor's Blog
New bureaus in China, Mexico and Berlin will soon add to CBC News's efforts to deliver international reporting by Canadians, for Canadians.
International reporting by Canadians, for Canadians, is essential amid shifting global alliances
We use this editor's blog to explain our journalism and what's happening at CBC News. You can find more blogs here.
On Monday, Nov. 2, CBC/Radio-Canada will celebrate its 90th birthday.

Founded in 1936, the Crown corporation was viewed by the Canadian government of the day as a necessary bulwark against a tsunami of U.S. culture, politics and information crossing our border via high-powered AM radio signals. (At the time, the Americans also controlled the majority of AM radio frequencies in North America, so the creation of the CBC was as much about Canadian identity as it was information sovereignty.)

Two important developments followed within the first five years of the public broadcaster’s birth: Canada declared war on Germany in 1939 and the CBC launched its own news division in 1941, ending its reliance on Canadian Press dispatches.

Before long, CBC journalists were sent overseas to cover the war, including the legendary correspondent Matthew Halton, whose battlefield reports are as compelling a listen today as they were when first broadcast in the early 1940s. Listen, for example, to his description of the Allied fight for Carpiquet in Normandy, in July 1944.

Halton did what the best of our international reporters do today (granted, he only had one medium to worry about). He reported facts with context and colour, he bore witness, he helped the listener understand the work behind his journalism — without making himself the centre of the story — from great distances and he brought stories to life for Canadians at home gathered around their radios.
That is still the mission of our journalists, delivered today across broadcast, web, apps, social platforms, podcasts and streaming services.
LISTEN | Halton reports on Carpiquet:
Archives8:11The battle for Carpiquet

International reporting by Canadians — for Canadians — is essential when shifting global alliances are redefining Canada’s place in the world order. And more than ever, global events have local consequences, as we’ve seen through a multitude of stories this past year, from the Strait of Hormuz to U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs to wars in the Middle East, Ukraine and Sudan, to the upcoming U.S. midterm elections.

CBC/Radio-Canada announced earlier this year plans to expand its international coverage, including opening (or reopening) permanent bureaus in Beijing, Jerusalem, Mexico City, Los Angeles and another European capital. We also intend to open a bureau in Africa in the next phase of this expansion.
New bureaus in China, Mexico and Berlin will soon add to CBC News's efforts to deliver international reporting by Canadians, for Canadians. (Greg Baker/AFP/Getty Images)

Currently, CBC News has bureaus in London, Mumbai, New York and Washington, D.C. Our French-language news service, Radio-Canada Info, has bureaus in Istanbul, Paris, Taipei and shares our space in Washington. We co-ordinate closely, share resources, and deploy to many more countries as news warrants. Last year news teams from CBC and Radio-Canada travelled to 65 countries.
But there is no replacement for having journalists permanently in place in different parts of the world. Here is the latest update on CBC’s efforts to expand its international presence:

items: I’m delighted to announce Lisa Xing will be our new Beijing-based correspondent covering China. Lisa has covered the Ontario Legislature, reported and hosted from Windsor and was part of CBC Toronto’s investigative team. She also covered the Beijing 2022 Winter Olympics. During more recent deployments to China, she produced reports on the country’s booming EV industry, the Chinese Communist Party's largest annual gathering and a trade mission by Canada’s finance minister.

I’m especially pleased to announce that Jorge Barrera will be our permanent correspondent in Mexico City. Jorge is a Venezuela-born journalist who previously worked with CBC's Investigative and Indigenous units. He has been in Mexico on a temporary deployment for a year now and produced some excellent journalism in that country, as well as in Cuba, Venezuela and Colombia. Among his recent work, he has documented Canadian health tourists seeking endometriosis treatment in Mexico, the kidnapping of workers from a Canadian mining firm, and a condo scam that snared an Ontario couple.

We are happy to announce our newest European bureau will be in Berlin and the correspondent job opening has just been posted. We chose Germany because it is a key economic and political anchor of the European Union, and Canada’s sixth-largest merchandise trading partner. The country’s ties to Canada have also been strengthened through recent agreements and promises to collaborate on critical minerals, AI, digital sovereignty, auto and battery manufacturing.

blocks.text: We hope to have more announcements soon on new correspondents and producers for Jerusalem, Beijing and Los Angeles, along with a new correspondent in our existing Mumbai bureau. Stay tuned!

In the meantime, please take a look at (or listen to) some of the remarkable international journalism our teams have produced in recent months, carrying on a decades-long tradition started by Matthew Halton and his peers. I think those first CBC correspondents would be proud of this work, and proud to know their legacy continues:

items: From on the ground in India: Frustrated Gen Zs and the Cockroach Party, a hero pilot celebrated in Mumbai, and what happens when a Google data centre moves in.

What will change for Canada if Republicans lose the U.S. midterms? (A recent hit episode from our popular new Washington bureau podcast Two Blocks from the White House.) Plus your guide to the midterms and why they matter.
24 hours in Kyiv: Living through Russian drone strikes.
How France was shaken by fiery street protests and whether the protests will change anything? More of our on-the-ground reporting here on TikTok.
What a long-serving Republican senator from a border state told us directly about Prime Minister Mark Carney’s efforts to strengthen ties with the European Union.
As settler violence erupted in the Occupied West Bank, CBC News was there.
We interviewed Cornell students as they marched in protest of the university’s handling of sexual assault case. And here’s an explainer on everything we know about the “Cornell 7.”

blocks.text: You can get the latest international reporting on the World section of our News site: cbc.ca/news/world
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Brodie Fenlon is general manager and editor in chief of CBC News.

articles.title: Gen Z protests in Germany: Is France-style violence looming?
articles.summary: Young people in Germany will take to the streets this weekend to demand education and action on climate change. Politicians warn that the protests could become violent, as in France, but the…

image.caption: Young people have already been protesting against the reintroduction of military serviceImage: Snowfield Photography/picture alliance

blocks.text: As politicians in Germany look ahead to the coming weekend, many fear that cities across the country could witness the kind of violent unrest that recently shook France. An initiative known as "Gen Z regelt" ("Gen Z sorts it") has launched a social media campaign calling for demonstrations in 23 cities nationwide.

"Gen Z" broadly refers to the generation born between 1995 and 2010. Many feel that their parents' generation has done too little to combat climate change and has allowed the gap between rich and poor to widen ever further. At the same time, they are concerned about their educational prospects and future opportunities in Western societies.
CDU: 'We must prevent scenes like those in France at all costs'

In France, what began as largely peaceful protests recently spiraled into serious unrest. Cars were set alight in several towns, while in Limoges the town hall was torched. In Lille, Lyon, and Toulouse and elsewhere, police deployed tear gas, leading to numerous arrests.
Many politicians, particularly within Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), are warning of similar scenes this coming weekend.
Alexander Throm, the CDU parliamentary group's domestic spokesperson, told the daily Handelsblatt newspaper: "Scenes like those in France must be prevented at all costs."
France protests continue despite police crackdown
Concerns over internationally coordinated far-left extremists
In Throm's view, far-left groups and criminals from immigrant communities could "hijack" the demonstrations. "An ominous alliance is emerging, particularly in Berlin," he warned.

Marc Henrichmann, also of the CDU, chair of the Bundestag's parliamentary oversight panel for the intelligence services, also expressed concern: "The far-left extremist scene is internationally connected and coordinated." He said that violent far-left activists now even cross national borders to engage in looting and acts of violence elsewhere.

But Sebastian Koos, sociologist at the University of Konstanz whose research focuses on youth and protest movements, told DW that he does not expect Germany to experience unrest on a scale comparable to that seen in France, even though events in the neighboring country helped spark the protests now being planned across Germany.
Koos: 'Not driven by anger as in France'

Koos sees key differences between young people in the two countries. "Unlike in France, these protests are not driven by the same level of anger," he said. "They have been planned, officially registered and carefully organized. The website, in particular, places strong emphasis on peaceful protest and repeatedly stresses a non-violent approach."

At the same time, the sociologist does not rule out the possibility that extremist groups could exploit the authorized demonstrations to stir up unrest: "It is certainly very important for the police and public authorities to be well prepared."

Quentin Gärtner, 19, studies biotechnology in Heidelberg and served until November of last year as secretary-general of the Federal Student Conference, which represents around 7.5 million school students in Germany.

"What unites us is that we have run out of patience with the education system. Many young people are deeply frustrated," he told DW. "The performance of German school students continues to decline, teaching positions are constantly being cut, and in many cases school buildings have seen little or no meaningful investment for years."

blocks.caption: Alexander Throm of the CDU has warned against far-left extremist violenceImage: Christoph Soeder/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Greens express understanding for the protests

For Gärtner, the discontent reflects a broader problem with parliamentary democracy in Germany and many other Western countries: "Politicians want to win elections. They focus on the groups that matter most to them electorally rather than on the future and the long-term sustainability of their policies," he said. "And in our aging societies, older people and the baby boomer generation are the groups that carry the most political weight."

Opposition parties in Germany have also voiced understanding for the concerns of younger people. Speaking to Germany's public broadcaster ZDF, Green Party co-leader Felix Banaszak said: "The intergenerational contract is no longer working. Older generations have driven the climate into a dead end."

He argued that the social welfare system was also reaching its limits and that rents had become unaffordable. According to Banaszak, the only thing the state seems to offer young people are the letters sent to 18-year-olds asking them to consider joining the military. Germany is currently desperate to expand the Bundeswehr and is considering reintroducing national service.

By Tuesday, around 134,000 people had registered on the "Gen Z regelt" website to take part in the protests planned for the coming Saturday. With several days still to go before the demonstrations, that number could rise further.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: US teen whose father arranged her marriage to Islamic State fighter convicted for weapons training
articles.summary:
‘You try to leave, it is death,’ Halima Salman testified. Her mother and defense attorneys wept after the verdict

A New York woman…

blocks.text: A New York woman whose father took her to Syria as a teenager and arranged her marriage to an Islamic State fighter was convicted on Tuesday of receiving weapons training from the militant group.

Prosecutors said Halima Salman, a US citizen, pledged loyalty to the extremist group and willingly participated in its activities. Jurors were shown a video of her holding an assault rifle, a photo of her with the group’s flag and loving text messages she sent her husband.
Brooklyn-based US attorney Joseph Nocella Jr said in a statement that the verdict held Salman “accountable for joining forces with a terrorist organization”.
The defense sought to portray Salman, now 27, as a teenager who was unwittingly trapped in Syria’s civil war, first by her father and later by an extremist husband whose orders she had to follow.
“You try to leave, it is death,” Salman testified. She said she refused to be “married off” at age 18 and repeatedly tried to get a divorce.

Salman, her mother and even her defense attorneys wept after hearing the verdict. Still in tears, Salman and her mother later hugged each other across the railing between the audience and the courtroom well.
Jurors, who began deliberating Thursday, had repeatedly indicated Monday that they were struggling to reach a unanimous decision. The members declined to comment as they left court after the verdict.

Salman’s lawyers also declined to comment. They are asking the judge to set aside the verdict and acquit her, as federal law allows if a judge finds the evidence presented at a trial doesn’t legally support a conviction. Such requests are often made but rarely granted.
Salman’s conviction carries the potential for up to 10 years in prison. Sentencing currently is set for 2 February.

The Islamic State group, which the US government designates as a terrorist group, seized large parts of Iraq and Syria in 2014 and declared the territory to be a caliphate. Despite its defeat in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria two years later, the group still has sleeper cells that carry out deadly attacks in both countries.

Born in Brooklyn, Salman was 17 when her father took the family on what she thought was a trip to visit relatives in Turkey in 2017. Instead, the van crossed into Syria, where masked gunmen surrounded them. Salman said she was frightened and confused and had no idea where her father was taking them.
“I do blame my father for a lot of things that happened,” she testified.
She said she spent three months in housing run by the Islamic State group before reuniting with her family. They moved twice because their homes were hit by airstrikes.
On the first day of her marriage, Salman recalled, her husband told her: “Get up, stupid wife, it’s time for you to be a wife.”
She spent much of the marriage doing domestic labor for her husband and mother-in-law. Her father died after being injured in an airstrike in 2018.

Prosecutors insisted Salman was dishonest and had more agency in Syria than she claimed. They got her to concede during cross-examination that she once sent a religious song about Osama bin Laden to her husband. Prosecutors also disputed Salman’s account of a poor marriage, citing two loving text messages she sent to her husband.

“The evidence shows that the defendant received military training from a violent, brutal, terrorist organization – an organization that is responsible for attacks across the world,” assistant US attorney Amanda Shami told the jury in a closing argument last week.

Salman’s husband took a video of her holding an assault rifle, which prosecutors said she had been trained to use. When she testified, Salman said she was only complying with her husband’s request to carry the rifle.
She recalled that her last year of marriage was particularly harrowing, as constant bombings sometimes forced them to live in the streets, where she recalled seeing “dead bodies everywhere”.
The couple eventually fled with other refugees in a truck, where she told her husband they were going to separate, and Salman testified that she never saw him again.
She was detained in Baghuz, Syria, in 2019 by forces opposed to the Islamic State group. She was arrested by US authorities when she returned to New York in 2024.

articles.title: Give UK workers right to know colleagues’ pay to prevent disparities, says watchdog
articles.summary:
EHRC says we need transparency if workers suspect other staff are being paid more for similar work

Workers should have a legal right to know their colleagues’ pay to help prevent pay…

blocks.text: Workers should have a legal right to know their colleagues’ pay to help prevent pay discrimination, particularly against women, the UK’s human rights watchdog has said.

The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) made the recommendation in response to government proposals to overhaul equal pay laws, saying workers deserved a right to transparency if they suspected other staff were being paid more for similar work.

The watchdog also said bosses should be banned from asking about applicants’ existing salaries when recruiting staff. Companies are currently allowed to request that information, but potential recruits do not have to respond.

Ministers are considering forcing bosses to respond to staff questionnaires about their colleagues’ pay, reintroducing a right that was abolished in 2014 as part of a drive to cut bureaucracy for businesses.

The EHRC said those forms should allow staff to request information about a colleague doing similar work, including annual salary and hours worked, as well as bonuses, overtime and their job description.
They should also be able to ask for details on any job evaluations carried out by bosses, revealing job grades, salary benchmarks, internal “scores” and a copy of any final job evaluation records.

They should also be able to ask for a ranking of each worker in a similar team, based on annual basic pay and hours, and have the right to push bosses for more information in cases where the data they receive is believed to be inaccurate or incomplete.
Crucially, the watchdog said bosses should be forced to respond within a “specified timeframe”.

The EHRC said: “Without such a requirement, employers may delay, provide evasive responses or avoid responding. We suggest this should be introduced as a mandatory measure, rather than an ‘optional’ one, to adequately meet the policy aims of this consultation.”
after newsletter promotion

Ultimately, boosting pay transparency could help companies avoid employment tribunals, resulting in “early resolution of pay disputes”, and help tackle the UK’s gender pay gap where women historically earn less than men, the EHRC said.

The median gender pay gap, as of April this year, shows that women in full-time work earned 6.8% less, on average, than men in the UK, according to the Office for National Statistics. However, that figure is wider across areas such as the finance industry, where the mean and median pay gaps, at 24% and 22% respectively, are double the national average for UK companies.

The EHRC said: “Introducing a requirement that prevents employers from asking about salary history or expectations, alongside the proposed pay transparency measures in this consultation, will likely reduce pay gaps and discrimination against women.”

articles.title: At least 64 people killed in Spain as 2 high-speed trains collide
articles.summary: 'We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail. Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train,' says a passenger…

blocks.text: COLLISION. Emergency teams work at the scene of a collision involving two high-speed trains near Urda station in Toledo province, Spain, on October 28, 2026.
Burak Akbulut/Anadolu

'We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail. Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train,' says a passenger traveling with several colleagues in the rear car of one of the trains

URDA, Spain – Rescue workers in Spain on Wednesday, October 28, were scouring the wreckage for more bodies at the crash scene where at least 64 people were killed when two high-speed trains collided, in the second deadly railway accident in the country this year.

Evacuated passengers streamed along a road near the scene, some splattered with blood or with their wounds bandaged, others wheeling suitcases and being given water by volunteers who said it had been donated from neighboring towns.

Hundreds of ambulances, funeral home vans and helicopters were parked next to a train with several carriages sitting on an elevated section of track while twisted metal, broken panels and wreckage could be seen strewn across an embankment beneath the line where at least three carriages had plunged.
Miguel, a passenger traveling with several colleagues in the rear car of one of the trains, described to COPE radio the moment of the accident.
“We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail. Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train,” he said.
A person briefed on the disaster said a train operated by private consortium Iryo stopped near Toledo on orders from infrastructure manager ADIF due to a signal fault.
A train operated by Renfe then struck the stationary train at high speed, causing several carriages of both trains to derail, the person said.
Renfe said in a statement that after a being authorized to continue its journey, its train had crashed into the Iryo train that had remained stationary “for reasons we don’t know.”

“The Renfe train continued on its way as instructed, and a collision occurred. The exact sequence of events, the traffic conditions and the circumstances of the impact will have to be established by the investigation,” Renfe said.
There was no immediate response to a Reuters request for comment from Iryo or Adif. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Budget 2026: John Healey offers £100 payment to households to help navigate ‘global economic storms’
articles.summary: Cash to 20m households part of package to help cut energy bills and ease cost-of-living crisis

blocks.text: John Healey promised to steer Britain through “global economic storms,” as he announced a package of measures to cut consumers’ energy bills in his first budget.

The chancellor said 20m households in council tax bands A to D would receive a £100 payment – a measure he said would cost £2.6bn. A VAT cut on electricity bills will be extended to next July, added Healey.
As widely expected, Healey cancelled fuel duty rises pencilled in by Rachel Reeves and announced he would echo her approach of shifting energy levies on to general taxation.

Earlier, Healey had announced that the gas standing charge would be abolished, perhaps as soon as next year – a move expected to cut utility bills for 60% of households, with the costs met by heavier users.
Healey blamed the ongoing war in the Middle East for the deterioration in the economic outlook since Reeves’s spring statement, but insisted he would keep Labour’s deficit-reduction plans on track.

“Analysts like to speak of economic headwinds, but what we face today are global economic storms,” he said, describing his statement as “a budget built on fiscal discipline, which matches immediate action today with clear direction for the future.”

He said higher inflation as a result of the Iran war was expected to cost the government £14bn more in interest costs and the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) had downgraded its growth forecast to 1% for next year, from the 1.6% it expected in the spring.

Nevertheless, Healey promised to meet Labour’s first fiscal rule, on balancing current spending with tax receipts by 2029-30; but with diminished headroom of £15bn – against the £24bn that Reeves set aside in March.
But he said the cushion would be rebuilt to £22bn, by 2030-31. “That is what a buffer is for. Use it when you need it, rebuild it when you can.”
As a result of continued high oil prices as a result of the Middle East conflict, the energy price cap, which determines household bills, is expected to increase sharply in January.
Healey signalled a radical reform to the way energy bills are charged in the longer term – calling it, “a new cost control framework, to drive down all aspects of energy bills.”
after newsletter promotion
Healey said the energy package would be funded by a windfall tax on Britain’s banks - as well as an unexpected 2 percentage-point tax rise for landlords and savers.
He said he would double the additional levy the banks pay on their profits, to 6% from the current 3%, for 15 months from January.

That fell short of the rise to 8% that industry figures had expected. Healey lavished praise on the sector, as he announced the measure. “I want to say directly to our banks: I celebrate and I am grateful for the role that you play,”he said.

articles.title: RFK Jr assailed over ‘wildly racist tirade’ about Arabs at Michigan campaign stop
articles.summary: US health secretary falsely claims at Mike Rogers rally that Arabs have never won major prizes in science or literature

blocks.text: Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, faced backlash on Wednesday for a “wildly racist tirade” during a campaign stop in Michigan in which he falsely asserted that Arabs never won major awards in science or literature.

Kennedy was speaking at the Monday night event in Grand Rapids in support of Mike Rogers, the Republican US Senate candidate who is trailing his Democratic midterms opponent Abdul El-Sayed, a Muslim, in polling.

“There’s 500 million Arabs in the world, and yet they don’t produce science, they don’t win the ⁠Nobel prize, they don’t win the Fields prize, they don’t win the Wolf prize, they don’t produce literature,” Kennedy said.
A factcheck published on Tuesday by the Associated Press showed that Arabs have won, or been short-listed, for all those awards in recent years.

The ⁠Council on American-Islamic Relations called Kennedy’s Islamophobic remarks “a ⁠textbook display of ​unvarnished racism and bigotry”, and the US healthcare advocacy organization Protect Our Care condemned his “wildly racist tirade”.
Hillary Scholten, a Democratic congresswoman representing west Michigan, who declined to endorse El-Sayed this summer, said Kennedy’s comments were “disgraceful and have no place in public service”.

In a statement posted to her Facebook page late Tuesday, Scholten said: “As secretary of health and human services, he has a responsibility to serve all Americans, not use his position to demean entire communities with bigoted and demonstrably false claims.

“Arab Americans are our neighbors, colleagues, health care professionals, scientists, educators, and public servants. Their contributions to science, literature, medicine, and countless other fields are undeniable.
“The last I checked, Secretary Kennedy has neither a medical degree nor a Nobel peace prize, and his rhetoric has undermined public confidence in health science. Maybe he should sit this one out.”
Kennedy’s comments came as part of an attack on the Muslim Brotherhood, a global Islamic group with branches that have been designated terrorist organizations by the US government.

The rise of the group had “created stagnant societies”, Kennedy said, ending what he called “a golden age [in which] Islamic lands were the center, the foundation for art and literature and science and engineering, and they were highly tolerant and pluralistic and cosmopolitan”.

Other Trump administration officials have tried to paint El-Sayed as a supporter of Islamic radicalism, including the president himself, who at a rally in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday called the Democrat “a jihadist” who was “on the side of the terrorists”.
after newsletter promotion

JD Vance, the vice-president, escalated the inflammatory attacks at an event in Howell, Michigan, on Tuesday, during which he sought to connect El-Sayed’s politics to violent leftwing protests in Paris that saw thousands arrested.

“I guarantee you, if those rioters were burning down New York, or Detroit, the Hasan Pikers and El-Sayeds would be right there leading them and cheering them on,” Vance said, referring to Piker, an outspoken socialist commentator and influencer.

Rogers has also spoken out against El-Sayed’s alleged links to the Muslim Brotherhood, despite questions over his own relationship with the group. In 2012, as chair of the House intelligence committee, he said the US should have talks with the movement after Mohamed Morsi, who was backed by the Muslim Brotherhood, won the Egyptian election.

El-Sayed has repeatedly denied any ties to the group, and disavowed it in a town hall event in Michigan last week that went viral for a confrontation over the issue with a heckler who turned out to be a former aide to Josh Hawley, the Republican US senator for Missouri.
Chris Murphy, the US senator for Connecticut who joined other senior Democratic politicians canvassing for El-Sayed in Michigan last week, also condemned Kennedy’s comments.
“I really think ​everyone needs to pay ‌attention to this coordinated campaign ​to delegitimize Muslim Americans, ​not just as citizens but as humans,” he said, reported by Reuters.

articles.summary: On September 28, 2025, Republic Act No. 12309, or the “Free Funeral Services Act,” lapsed into law after 30 days without President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.'s signature. This law institutionalized the…

blocks.text: Did you know that the government is mandated by law to provide free funeral services to poor Filipinos who cannot afford a decent burial for their loved ones?
On September 28, 2025, Republic Act No. 12309, or the “Free Funeral Services Act,” lapsed into law after remaining unacted upon for 30 days without the signature of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
This law institutionalized the Department of Social Welfare and Development’s (DSWD) funeral assistance initiative through its Aid to Individuals in Crisis Situation (AICS) program.

Under RA 12309, free funeral services must be extended to families in crisis situations, as determined by the DSWD, including indigent families, those affected by calamities or disasters, and individuals facing emergency circumstances that prevent them from affording dignified burial services.
How does the law grant its beneficiaries a decent funeral?
Beneficiary
According to the Free Funeral Services Act, the service is provided to “poor families per death of a family member.”
The law defines “poor families” as those whose income falls below the poverty threshold as defined by the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development.
This classification also includes those unable to meet basic needs, such as food, health, education, and housing, as defined under the Social Reform and Poverty Alleviation Act.

For 2025, the poverty threshold was set at a national average of P14,634 per month, up from P13,873 in 2023. Meaning, this figure represents the minimum income required for a family to meet its basic food and non-food needs.
Under this 2025 threshold, a family whose monthly income falls below the threshold is considered poor.
How to avail the assistance?
Free funeral services may be obtained from accredited funeral establishments nationwide that offer a standardized indigent funeral package.
“Free funeral services shall be provided to poor families per death of a family member by accredited funeral establishment anywhere in the country,” the law said.

Funeral establishments refer to licensed businesses that provide services such as funeral parlors, chapels, and similar facilities used for preparing, transporting, storing, and caring for the deceased prior to burial or cremation.
The free funeral package covers the preparation of funeral documents, embalming, burial, cremation, inurnment, transportation, and the provision of a casket or urn.
To avail of the indigent funeral package, under the law, the bereaved family or an authorized representative must present the following requirements:

items: Valid identification card of the claimant or beneficiary;
Death certificate issued by the hospital or city/municipal health office, or certification from the tribal chieftain;
Funeral contract signed by the representative of the deceased's family, the funeral establishment, and an authorized DSWD personnel; and
Social care study prepared by any registered social worker

blocks.text: At present, the DSWD also requires additional documents depending on the specific services requested. Further details are available through the DSWD AICS Funeral Assistance Portal.
Upon the approval of the DSWD Regional Director, the agency pays the funeral establishment for the indigent package rendered to the beneficiary.

“The payment will be based on the stipulations of the signed contract between the representative of the deceased's family, the funeral establishment, and the authorized DSWD personnel,” the law notes.
Penalties for violations
Funeral establishments that refuse to provide free funeral services face a maximum fine of P400,000, alongside the revocation of their operating license.
Meanwhile, individuals who fraudulently avail of the free funeral service face up to six months of imprisonment and a maximum fine of P500,000.

Data from the DSWD show that from 2014 to September 2025, the agency extended burial assistance to families of 1,439,160 individuals, releasing a total of P10.9 million through the AICS program. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc in slight lead with more than 80% of votes counted
articles.summary: While partial results show the pro-Netanyahu bloc ahead of the anti-Netanyahu bloc, the final tally could take days. Neither grouping is expected to win a majority, with tough coalition talks ahead.…
articles.byline: Patrick Große, Mark Hallam, Felix Tamsut, Roshni Majumdar, Matt Ford

image.caption: Supporters of the main opposition party Yashar celebrate after exit polls suggested they were on course to win 21 seatsImage: Jack Guez/AFP

blocks.text: October 28, 2026
Situation barely moves as more than 80% of vote counted

Partial results published by the Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel newspaper showed the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on 54 seats, with 84.5% of votes counted.
The opposition bloc under Gadi Eisenkot of the centrist Yashar party was on 49 seats.
Neither bloc is set to received the 61 seats need for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, making some form of coalition likely.
The Arab-led parties — the Joint List and the United Arab List, commonly known under its Hebrew name of Ra’am — have dropped to 17 seats.
The numbers are still likely to change, particularly after a record number of absentee votes are counted.
The full tally of those will possibly not be confirmed until Friday, according to the newspaper.

articles.title: Australia must recruit hundreds more to crew Aukus submarines, retired admiral warns
articles.summary:
As USS Colorado showcases the program in Perth, Peter Briggs says personnel is just one of the ‘huge issues’ it faces

  • Get our

blocks.text: Australia faces an uphill battle to recruit and train enough naval personnel to serve on submarines planned for the future fleet of nuclear-powered vessels under the controversial $368bn Aukus deal, a retired admiral has warned.

As the Virginia-class submarine USS Colorado arrived at HMAS Stirling south of Perth on Tuesday for a month of routine maintenance and to help build Australian expertise, retired admiral Peter Briggs said more people needed to be enrolled in the navy’s submarine program.

As part of a $368bn trilateral defence deal, Australia will acquire between three and five Virginia-class, nuclear-powered submarines from the United States to replace its five diesel-electric Collins-class vessels, which are becoming obsolete.
The new submarines are much bigger and require up to 134 crew – almost three times the number needed for the Collins class.
The Royal Australian Navy says it has 230 personnel in various stage of the US nuclear-powered submarine training pipeline.

blocks.caption: Captain Justin Reeves talks to the media on USS Colorado at HMAS Stirling in Perth. Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAP

blocks.text: “Of these, approximately 145 have completed US Naval nuclear power training and are now building experience training on US Navy SSNs [a hull classification for nuclear-powered submarines],” a navy spokesperson said.
“By 2030, we expect to have 400 Royal Australian Navy officers and sailors trained and ready to serve.”
But Briggs urged a more intensive recruitment plan to crew the bigger boats.
“We have got to triple the size of the submarine arm and we’ve got to train them in nuclear skills,” he said.
“You are heading toward needing a submarine arm of 3,000, that’s the hill you have to climb.”
Approximately 850 submariners are qualified to operate Collins-class vessels.
The Virginia-class boats are intended to bridge the transition from the Collins-class fleet to the future SSN-AUKUS submarine, an even bigger design being developed by Australia and the UK.

blocks.caption: Crew members on the USS Colorado. Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAP

blocks.text: “The personnel side is a huge issue, but it’s not the only one,” Briggs said.
The former submariner argued that maintaining two different submarine types would add complexity to training, logistics, maintenance and spare-parts arrangements.
The Australian government did not respond to questions about recruitment targets and whether a workforce development program was on track.
Recruitment is further complicated by the need for more than a dozen different trades, from radio and sonar operators to cooks and electricians.

After spending the next month is Perth, the USS Colorado will return to the city’s waters again in late 2027 as part of the Submarine Rotational Force-West program which is designed to help Australia build the skills and infrastructure to operate its own nuclear fleet.
From 2027, the program will see up to four US and one UK nuclear-powered submarine rotate through HMAS Stirling.

Paul Johnson, HMAS Stirling fleet base west commodore, said the USS Colorado maintenance period would be used to “practise and test our procedures across a range of nuclear-related operational scenarios”.
Officials stressed that no radiological material would be transferred during the maintenance period and that nuclear-related exercises would be simulated.
Late last year, Senate estimates heard that US submarines carrying nuclear weapons could rotate through Australian ports despite a non-proliferation commitment.
USS Colorado captain, Justin Reeves, said the US government would not “confirm or deny the presence of nuclear weapons on specific platforms”.
Colorado was built in 2018 and arrived this week carrying conventional weapons, including four torpedoes and four “payload tubes” that can be used to house and launch weapons.

It took two weeks to travel to Perth from Pearl Harbor in Hawaii with 160 men and no women aboard. A sign labelled “Berth Rules”, taped to the wall near the submarine’s entryway, listed “Don’t be stinky” as the crew’s top priority once they reach port.

blocks.caption: Sleeping quarters on the USS Colorado. Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAP

blocks.text: The demands of living and working in confined spaces for extended periods presents another recruitment challenge for officials.
Sleeping arrangements can involve bunks stacked three high, while “hot racking” allows three sailors to share two beds by rotating their sleeping schedules around watch duties.
In some circumstances, and when accommodation is limited, sailors may sleep in torpedo rooms.
Reeves said the vessel is “built for combat, not for comfort”.
Nuclear submarines don’t need to refuel, meaning their range is effectively infinite. “The limits of its endurance are really food and toilet paper, and that’s several months’ worth,” Reeves said.
“Being nuclear powered is a massive advantage.”

The Commission on Elections (Comelec) will resume voter registration on November 10 ahead of the 2028 national and local elections, Chairperson George Garcia said on Wednesday.
Garcia said the registration period would run until July 30, 2027.

“Sa mga kababayan natin na gustong magparehistro dahil hindi sila rehistrado, magpa-revive ng registration, magpa-transfer ng kanilang registration, o kaya naman magpa-reactivate ng kanilang registration, o magpabago sa kahit anong datos doon, gawin nyo po 'yan mula November 10 at ito po ay tatagal hanggang sa next year, as much as possible July 30,” Garcia told reporters.

(Those who wish to register as voters, reactivate or transfer their registration, or update any information in their records may do so starting November 10. The registration period is expected to last until July 30 next year.)
The poll body earlier said around 74 million Filipinos are expected to be eligible to vote in the May 2028 national and local elections.
Comelec also projected that an additional one million voters would be eligible to vote in the November 2028 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE). — Vince Angelo Ferreras/VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Alex Eala advances to Toray Pan Pacific quarterfinals after besting Talia Gibson
articles.summary: Eala is now set to face Russian player Diana Shnaider, who previously defeated her in the second round of the Ningbo Open in China

blocks.text: FILIPINA TENNIS STAR. Alex Eala at the Toray Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo, Japan.
Toray Pan Pacific Open website
Eala is now set to face Russian player Diana Shnaider, who previously defeated her in the second round of the Ningbo Open in China
MANILA, Philippines – Alex Eala pulls off a triumphant win over Australia’s Talia Gibson, 4-6, 6-2, 6-0, in the Toray Pan Pacific Open round of 16 match in Tokyo, Japan, on Wednesday, October 28.

Eala had gotten off to a rough start after losing the first set to her World No. 38 opponent, 4-6. It had been smooth sailing in the succeeding sets, 6-2, 6-0, as she was able to contain Gibson by a large margin.
“I think really staying in the match [and] never giving up,” Eala explained in a post-game interview when asked what the key to her victory was.
“The first set was difficult, and I had my chances, so I knew that if I kept my concentration I would have more chances.”

This is not the first time the two players went head-to-head with each other. Eala and Gibson had previously played against each other at the IXXVII Open Generali Ciudad de Palma del Rio round of 16 in June 2023, and then in the ITF W25 Aldershot GB Pro Series round of 16 in August 2023. The Filipina won both matches.
The Filipina tennis star will now face Diana Shnaider of Russia in the quarterfinals on Friday, October 30.
Just before Eala made her Toray Pan Pacific Open debut, she had suffered a second-round exit at the hands of Shnaider at the Ningbo Open in China on October 22. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Toxics watchdog urges parents to avoid unauthorized squishy toys for safety
articles.summary: A Toxics Watchdog has issued a reminder to parents and consumers on Tuesday to refrain from purchasing unauthorized squishy toys to reduce the risk of toxic exposure among children.

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 8:34pm
A Toxics watchdog has issued a reminder to parents and consumers on Tuesday to refrain from purchasing unauthorized squishy toys to reduce the risk of toxic exposure among children.

BAN Toxics took note of the public health advisories posted by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) against the purchase and use of unauthorized Toy and Childcare Article (TCCA) products, ‘Squishy Delicious’ toys.

"The FDA advisory follows an earlier consumer alert by BAN Toxics over food-like squeezy dumpling toys that have gained popularity online. Resembling steamed buns, these products continue to be sold in retail stores and through online shopping platforms," the group said.
The toys are available in different sizes and colors, some contain glitter, and cost from P80 to P200 in retail stories and between P60 to P150 through online shopping sites.
It can be recalled that the FDA issued its advisories in September on the purchase and use of the unauthorized squishy toys Squishy Delicious Blue and Squishy Delicious Green.
The purchase and use of the toys are unauthorized because these have not been issued the required Certificate of Product Notification (CPN).
Potential hazards
"Since the toys have not undergone the FDA notification process, the agency cannot assure their quality and safety," the group said.

"Potential hazards may arise from ingredients that are not permitted in toy and childcare article products. The use of substandard and possibly adulterated products may pose health risks, including endocrine disruption and reproductive or developmental effects, as well as injuries, choking, or suffocation due to small or broken parts," they added.
There were reported product recalls in the UK and US, for squishy dumpling toys "due to excessive concentrations of benzene, posing a serious chemical risk to children’s health and safety."

According to the UK Office for Product Safety and Standards, “The product presents a serious chemical risk because the outer layer contains an excessive concentration of benzene (20 mg/kg). If inhaled, benzene can cause irritation to the eyes, nose, and throat. Exposure to large amounts may also cause a burning sensation in the digestive tract and skin irritation.”
Health effects

Ban Toxics cited a statement issued by the World Health Organization (WHO) that “Human exposure to benzene has been associated with a range of acute and long-term adverse health effects and diseases, including cancer and haematological effects. Exposure can occur occupationally, in the general environment, and in the home as a result of the widespread use of benzene-containing petroleum products.”

The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) issued Administrative Order No. 2026-29 on the Chemical Control Order for Benzene, which stated that this chemical should not be used in toys and other children’s products.

“We laud the FDA and the DENR for their regulatory actions against unauthorized toys that may contain chemicals that pose risks to a child’s health and development,” said Thony Dizon, Advocacy and Campaign Officer of BAN Toxics.
“It is high time for government agencies to enforce the law and immediately recall and remove the products from the market.”

Ban Toxics also cited Republic Act No. 10620 or the Toy and Game Safety Labeling Act of 2013, which provides that all toys and games, whether locally manufactured or imported, distributed, donated, or sold in the Philippines, must comply with the applicable safety labeling and manufacturer’s marking requirements under the Philippine National Standards (PNS) for toy safety. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Dementia cases in US projected to rise dramatically by 2050, study finds
articles.summary:
Increase will add strain on healthcare system already struggling amid cuts by Trump administration, experts say

The number of people with dementia in the United States is projected to…

blocks.text: The number of people with dementia in the United States is projected to increase dramatically over the next 25 years, which will place increasing strain on a healthcare system already struggling to help them amid cuts by the Trump administration, experts say.

According to a new study in Jama Neurology, the annual incidence of new dementia cases globally will more than double, from 11.4m in 2023 to 24.7m in 2050. In the United States, the number of adults diagnosed with dementia each year will increase from 514,000 in 2020 to 1m by 2060, according to a Jama study published in 2024.

The United States already does not have enough geriatric specialists or people working in home care and at nursing homes. The Trump administration has also significantly cut funding for Medicaid, which covers a substantial portion of long-term care.

Those gaps mean the country must focus on preventing dementia, discovering new drugs to at least delay its onset and recruiting people for the demanding jobs of providing care for individuals with Alzheimer’s, people in the field say.

“Families will be absorbing enormous emotional and financial costs … because dementia often requires years of increasing supervision and hands-on care, which our healthcare system is not really designed to provide,” said Jordan Weiss, an assistant professor at the Optimal Aging Institute at NYU Langone.

The number of people with dementia is projected to increase because life expectancy has gone up in recent decades, which means larger numbers of people are entering the age brackets in which dementia is most common. Also, in the United States, the Hispanic population almost doubled between 2000 and 2024, and that demographic is 1.5 times as likely to develop dementia as white people, according to the Alzheimer’s Association.

“Even if you reduce the risk of dementia, just the sheer number of adults who are entering the ages where dementia is most common will increase the number of people living with and who develop dementia,” Weiss said.

Meanwhile, nursing homes are struggling to meet the existing demand. Almost all facilities reported difficulty recruiting new staff and two-thirds said a primary issue was a lack of interested or qualified candidates, according to a 2024 report from the American Health Care Association, a nursing home lobbying group. About half reported that they had limited new admissions of residents.

“We are asking workers to perform what are very physically and emotionally demanding jobs. Helping people bathe, eat, dress and navigate cognitive decline, often for relatively low wages, unpredictable hours, and limited opportunities for advancement,” Weiss said.

The country’s need for nursing assistants and home health aides is expected to increase by 48% and 42% between 2020 and 2035, according to the Center for American Progress. And yet, the median wage in May 2025 for nursing assistants at assisted living facilities and in home healthcare was less than $19 an hour, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The median wage for home health aides was $17 an hour.

“The retention rate of those direct care workers is really, really low because it’s really difficult work. You can’t replace that with AI, and they are not getting adequately reimbursed,” said Regina Shih, a professor of epidemiology at Emory University who studies dementia and caregiving.

Meanwhile, the number of people becoming geriatric doctors has actually decreased in recent decades. In 2000, there were 10,270 geriatricians in the US; in 2022, there were only 7,413, according to a Jama report. It is among the lowest-paid medical specialties.
“I think it in part is related to compensation,” and “I just think residency interest hasn’t necessarily kept pace with some other fields,” Weiss said.
States are taking steps to try to address the labor shortages. In 2025, almost half reported offering incentive payments to recruit or retain Medicaid home care workers, according to a KFF survey.
South Carolina created a loan forgiveness program for physicians who complete fellowships in geriatrics or geriatric psychiatry and practice in the state for at least five years.

But states must also now contend with Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which passed in 2025 and included nearly $1tn in cuts to Medicaid spending over 10 years. Medicaid pays for more than half of what the country spends on long-term care, KFF reports.

“It’s a serious challenge for expanding access” to the growing number of people with dementia “who are eligible for Medicaid to get services like home care, personal care aid, respite care”, Shih said.

There have, however, been positive developments in geriatric medicine. In recent years, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved two drugs, Kisunla and Leqembi, that can modestly slow cognitive decline among some patients with early Alzheimer’s disease. The agency has also recently approved blood tests that can help diagnose the disease – and perhaps even predict if they are likely to develop it.

“It may improve people’s lives, and it may do a lot for how we slow decline or think about prevention, but it will be costly” for the healthcare system, said Julie Zissimopoulos, a University of Southern California professor and principal investigator of the US Cost of Dementia Project.
Given that a cure for Alzheimer’s does not appear to be imminent, it is important that we don’t just wait for one, Weiss said.

“We have a real opportunity to reduce dementia risk through better cardiovascular health [and] physical activity,” Weiss said. “Scientific breakthroughs matter, but so does building a healthcare system and infrastructure capable of delivering the care that people already need.”
